title: One meal, one breath
hookLine: live like it's your last day, say the mugs; the Buddha praised something smaller (AN 6.19)
tomorrow: why would anyone think about death at sunset, on purpose?

lines: LIVE LIKE IT'S YOUR LAST DAY.
cards: Live every day like it's your last. It's on mugs, posters, graduation cards. The Buddha once asked his monks a version of the same question, and he didn't praise the day.
One monk said a day. Others went smaller, down to a single meal. The Buddha praised the smallest answers: one mouthful, one breath.

teach.h: A DAY, A MEAL, A MOUTHFUL.
teach.b: It's the same sutta as yesterday, in the Anguttara Nikaya. How do you practice mindfulness of death? One monk: I think, may I live a day and a night, to attend to the teaching; I'd have done much.
Another: a day. Another: the time of one meal. Another: a few mouthfuls.
Another: one mouthful. And the last: the time to breathe in after breathing out. The Buddha calls the long stretches heedless, slow.
The one mouthful and the one breath are heedful. So which stretch should a person hold? Teachers have leaned two ways, and both views have roots in the suttas.
The first says: take the sutta straight.
One breath means no postponing, ever; urgency is the medicine, because the eighty-percent feeling always says later. The second says: careful.
The same Buddha told a monk named Sona, who had pushed himself until his feet bled, that effort is like the strings of a lute. Too tight, no music. Too loose, no music.
Tuned, it plays. Urgency without balance burns out. Here's where they meet.
A breath isn't a deadline to cram into. It's the smallest piece of life you can actually use. You can't fix your whole life in one breath.
You can be present for one.
That's the heedfulness the Buddha praised: not panic, attention.
Not a last day, a next breath.

how: Many meditation teachers use AN 6.19's 'one breath' as a reminder to come back to the present breath; others pair it with the Buddha's lute-string advice to Sona, so the reflection stays steady rather than strained.

o: a vow to eat only once a day during a retreat
the last meal the Buddha ate before he died
a monk's reflection: may I live the length of a meal

games.q: the monks' answers — tap the pairs.
p: too tight or too loose, no music

s: the Buddha praised the monk who said 'live as if it's your last day'
he called the day-long stretch heedless and praised one mouthful and one breath.
the Buddha compared balanced effort to a tuned lute string
to Sona: too tight, no music; too loose, no music; tuned, it plays.
the one breath means cramming as much as possible into every moment
a breath is the smallest piece of life you can use: be present for it, not rushed.

games.q: you love the one-breath reading: no postponing, ever. a friend says it makes her anxious. what's her strongest case, from inside the tradition?
o: death reflection is only for monks, so lay people can skip it.
the Buddha told Sona effort is like a lute string: too tight won't play.
the sutta praises the monk who reflects on a whole day and night.
games.why: her best case is the Buddha's own: balance. both views meet in attention: one breath, present, tuned rather than tight.

practice: Sit upright, the way you'd sit if this breath mattered, hands resting easy. Breathe in, and as you breathe out, let the thought be: one breath more, to practice. Then let each next breath come on its own, tuned, not tight.

wordCard.voice: One meal: the monk who reflected, may I live the length of one meal, to practice. Good, the Buddha said, and one breath is better still.

orig.note: Pali: heedfulness, not wasting time; the quality the Buddha praises in the one-breath monk.

carryVoice: Your line: one breath more, not one more day. Tuned, not tight. Day sixteen twenty-seven, one breath at a time.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 6.19 (Maranassati Sutta: the monks' answers from a day and night to one breath; the Buddha praises the mouthful and the breath as heedful)
Anguttara Nikaya 6.55 (Sona Sutta: the simile of the lute strings)
